n: This book is a revelation from Jesus Christ, given by the Father and delivered through an angel to John. “Revelation” translates the Greek apokalypsis—an unveiling of hidden things.
John faithfully recorded God’s word, Christ’s testimony, and everything he saw in vision.
The first of seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation: those who read this prophecy aloud, those who hear it, and those who live by it will be blessed.

f.g: In early churches one person read scripture aloud to the congregation.

n: John greets seven real congregations in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey). The blessing comes from the eternal God and from the “seven Spirits” before His throne—seven being a number of completeness.

f.w: seven churches which are in Asia
f.g: Seven cities in the Roman province of Asia, not the continent.

f.w: which is, and which was, and which is to come

n: Grace also comes from Jesus Christ: the faithful witness, the first to rise from the dead, and ruler of earth’s kings. John praises Him who loves us and washed away our sins with His own blood.

f.w: washed us from our sins in his own blood

n: Christ has made His followers kings and priests to serve God. Latter-day Saints associate this with temple blessings and exaltation.
Christ will come again in the clouds, and everyone will see Him—even those who pierced Him. All earth’s peoples will mourn.
The Lord declares that He is Alpha and Omega—the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. He is the beginning and the end, the Almighty.
John describes himself as a fellow believer sharing their suffering. He had been banished to Patmos, a small rocky island in the Aegean Sea, because of his testimony.

f.g: A small island off the coast of modern Turkey, used by Rome for exile.

n: On the Lord’s day—Sunday, the day of Christ’s Resurrection—John was caught up in the Spirit and heard a voice behind him loud as a trumpet.
The voice told John to write what he saw and send it to seven named churches. The cities lie roughly in a circle, in the order a messenger would travel.

f.g: The last stop on the circuit, near Colossae.

n: Turning toward the voice, John saw seven golden lampstands.

f.g: Lampstands holding oil lamps, not candles.

n: Among the lampstands stood one like the Son of Man—Jesus—in a long robe with a golden sash across His chest, like a priest or king.
His hair was white as wool and snow, and His eyes blazed like fire. These images show purity, eternal wisdom, and the power to see through everything.
His feet glowed like polished bronze in a furnace, and His voice sounded like a roaring waterfall. Joseph Smith described the resurrected Lord in the Kirtland Temple in similar terms.
He held seven stars in His right hand, a sharp two-edged sword came from His mouth, and His face shone like the noonday sun.

f.g: His word, which judges and cuts to the heart.

n: John collapsed like a dead man. Jesus touched him and said, “Don’t be afraid. I am the first and the last.”

f.w: fell at his feet as dead

n: Jesus declares that He died and now lives forever, holding the keys of death and hell. Because of Him, death and the spirit prison will not have the last word.

f.w: keys of hell and of death
f.g: hell = Greek hadēs, the realm of the dead.

n: Christ tells John to write what he has seen, what currently is, and what will happen later.
Jesus explains the symbols: the seven stars are the “angels” or messengers of the churches—likely their leaders—and the lampstands are the churches themselves, which are to give light.

f.g: Greek angelos — messenger; probably the presiding officers of each congregation.
